newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sweden, eye on election, sets bullish budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sweden, eye on election, sets bullish budget.

text.p: Sweden on Tuesday announced an expansionary budget, committing the state to spending more than 66 billion crowns ($8.6 billion) over the next four years to pump-prime the economy.
After two and a half years of austerity since taking office in September 1994, the minority Social Democratic Party government announced a five-point programme aimed at slashing unemployment.

"There's light at the end of the tunnel for Sweden," Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told parliament as he unveiled the supplementary budget, which outlined state spending plans until the end of the century.
Asbrink said the new money would be used to restore cuts in Sweden's welfare service which have severely damaged the government's popularity and halve unemployment.
The political nature of the budget was underlined by Labour Minister Margareta Winberg, who said it would be crucial to the campaign for next year's general election.
"This is an aggressive budget that will be handy to have as we go into the election campaign. It will represent the foundation for a successful campaign," she said.
The budget proposed spending 5.5 billion crowns in 1997, 16.3 billion crowns in 1998, 21.0 billion in 1999 and 23.3 billion in 2000, a total of 66.1 billion crowns.
A large part of the spending would go on labour market measures and on Sweden's social services, including more money spent on education and infrastructure projects.

"The proposed measures are estimated to lead to unemployment falling to 4.5 percent in 2000," the government said, acknowledging it would not quite achieve the radical goal of 4.0 percent unemployment it set itself.
Unemployment in Sweden was running at 8.4 percent in March.
Despite the dramatic spending plans, the government acknowledged that economic growth was modest and downgraded slightly the forecasts it presented in a budget last September.

The government said it saw year-on-year consumer prices rising 1.8 percent in 1997 and 1.5 percent in 1998, compared to a price fall of 0.2 percent in 1996. It had earlier forecast a 2.2 percent rise for both this year and next year.
GDP was expected to rise 2.3 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998, the government said, leaving the forecast for next year unchanged and downgrading its 1998 estimate from 2.6 percent.

The minority Social Democratic government also said it saw a state borrowing need of 26 billion crowns in 1997 and of nine billion crowns in 1998, compared to a 1996 central government borrowing of 21.0 billion crowns.

The government said exports would grow 6.3 percent in 1997, with growth tailing off to 5.1 percent in the year 2000. Imports were expected to show a slowly rising trend, growing by 5.0 percent in 1997.
Private consumption in Sweden rose by 1.5 percent in 1996 and is expected to rise by a modest 2.0 percent in 1997 and 1998.
The government said real wage increases were the highest in 1996 for 20 years and wages were expected to increase by 4.7 percent this year and by 3.5 percent next year.
Inflation, seen as the government's big success story, was seen staying below two percent for the next two years.
The bullish state of Sweden's finances seemed to have surprised the government.
"The deficit in general government finances has during 1996, despite weaker economic growth, declined at an unexpectedly rapid rate," the finance ministry said in a statement.
Budget balance is expected to be reached in 1998 and a surplus afterwards, which will finance a large part of the spending plans published on Tuesday.
The government also said, however, that it had shelved demands that Swedish local authorities should balance their books.
($ = 7.663 Swedish Crowns)
